title: Thiebou Nop Niébé, Black-Eyed Peas with Rice
author: Lois Sinaiko Webb
desc: Overnight-soaked black-eyed peas simmered with a smoked ham hock until tender, then mixed with the picked meat and a cup of cooked rice.
longDesc: A side dish from the Multicultural Cookbook of Life-Cycle Celebrations, reprinted by the Madison Returned Peace Corps Volunteers. A pound of dried black-eyed peas soaks overnight; the soaking water is discarded; the peas simmer covered in 6 cups of water with a half pound of smoked ham hocks, a chopped onion and a teaspoon of ground red pepper for 1 to 1 1/2 hours until tender. The hocks are skinned and the meat cut small, returned with a cup of cooked rice, and heated over medium for 5–7 minutes. The page serves it with lamb and salad.
ingredients: 1 tsp ground red pepper, more or less to taste
steps: Soak the peas in water overnight. Drain and discard the soaking water.
Cover the peas with 6 cups of water and add the ham hocks, onion and red pepper. Bring to a boil, then simmer covered 1 to 1 1/2 hours, until the peas and meat are tender.
Remove the hocks, discard the skin and cut the meat into small pieces.
Return the meat to the pot with the cooked rice and heat over medium 5 to 7 minutes.
chefTips: Tender peas and tender meat are the only cue; check at an hour.
Discard the soaking water — the page says so.
The page presents this as a side, to serve with lamb and salad.
commonMistakes: Salting early and toughening the peas (a general cook’s rule, not printed).
reheating: Gently with a splash of water.
healthBenefits: Black-eyed peas supply fibre, folate and plant protein.
A smoked ham hock adds sodium and saturated fat in small amounts per serving.
culturalNote: The spelling ‘nop niébé’ — the ‘nop’ element appears in no other source in this collection for thiebou niébé; it is recorded as printed and not normalised. The page notes the recipe takes two days.
sources: Credit line as printed: ‘Recipe from Multicultural Cookbook of Life-Cycle Celebrations, by Lois Sinaiko Webb.’ Published on the Returned Peace Corps Volunteers of Madison 2019 International Calendar page. No page date. Yield: ‘Serves 6–8’ (7 used here). The page says the recipe takes 2 days. TWO-PASS.

Cue in a short fragment: peas and meat ‘tender’, after 1 to 1 1/2 hours. Only the 5–7 minutes at the end and the overnight soak are other times. Rest time here is the overnight soak, entered as 12 hours.
NAME NOTE: the page spells it ‘Thiebou nop niébé’; the ‘nop’ appears in no other source for thiebou niébé.

Of the same page’s other recipes, the méchoui (450°F sear, then 325°F, thermometer about 150°F for medium) has the only oven temperatures in the whole Senegal research and is not entered as a recipe here.
